source.version: Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013 (SSRN 4573321), dated September 22, 2023, 58 pages. Not the Organization Science (2026) version of record, which was not available.
source.title_on_document: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality

supplement.where: The paper refers to no separate online supplement. Appendices A to E are inside this PDF (PDF pp. 44-58). The pre-registration (osf.io/ytaev) is embargoed and 'available from the authors upon request' (PDF p. 9, fn 2).
supplement.holds: Appendix D (PDF p. 53) says creativity ratings (1 to 10) of each subject's idea list are presented 'in Table 1', but no such table appears in Appendix D or anywhere else in this PDF. The similarity results are shown only as density plots (Figure 6, PDF p. 36; Appendix D Figure 1, PDF p. 53), with no means, SEs, or tests printed.

paper_design_summary: Boston Consulting Group consultants (758 completed) were split into two separate experiments. In each, they first did a baseline task without AI, then were randomly assigned to no AI, GPT-4 access (GPT Only), or GPT-4 access plus a prompt-engineering overview (GPT + Overview). In the 'inside the frontier' experiment (385 consultants) they developed a new shoe product across 18 questions (ideation, analysis, writing, persuasion), graded by two human graders and by GPT-4; the shoe ideas from question 1 were also embedded with the Universal Sentence Encoder to measure similarity across subjects. In the 'outside the frontier' experiment (373 consultants) they solved a business case scored for correctness and recommendation quality.

studies.label: Inside-the-frontier experiment (creative product innovation: new shoe concept, 18 questions)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to GPT-4 (none, GPT Only, GPT + prompt-engineering overview) for the experimental task, after a baseline task done without AI. Assignment was stratified on gender, location, tenure, openness to innovation, and native English status.
assignment.quote: Following this, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions to assess the influence of AI on their tasks, with these conditions being consistent across both experiments.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 7), Section 2 Methods; stratification at PDF p. 10 (printed p. 6)
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 5), Section 2, footnote 2: OSF osf.io/ytaev, embargoed

arms.name: Control
arms.description: No AI support on the experimental task.

arms.name: GPT Only
arms.description: Access to a GPT-4 chat tool on a company platform built on the OpenAI API.

arms.name: GPT + Overview
arms.description: Same GPT-4 tool plus a prompt-engineering overview (instructional videos and documents on effective use).

participants.exclusions: Of 852 consultants who answered the enrollment survey, 758 completed the experiment (PDF p. 9, fn 3); 385 of them were in this experiment. The paper does not say whether the 94 non-completers were randomized or in which experiment or arm they were. Per-arm counts are not reported. Tables 1-3 report 385 observations.
participants.who: Individual-contributor strategy consultants at Boston Consulting Group (about 7 percent of that cohort worldwide).
participants.country: Multiple (BCG offices around the world; no country breakdown given)
participants.quote: Approximately half of the participants (385 consultants) tackled a series of tasks where they were prompted to conceptualize and develop new product ideas
participants.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 6), Section 2; Table 1, PDF p. 38 (Observations 385)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 (as available at end of April 2023), default system prompt and temperature, through a company platform built on the OpenAI API that mirrors ChatGPT
ai_tool.how_used: Free interactive chat with GPT-4 during the 90-minute experimental task. Prompts and responses were logged. Appendix C shows most AI users largely copied GPT-4 output into their answers (modal retainment about 0.87).

task.description: Develop a new shoe for an underserved market or sport through 18 questions: generate at least 10 ideas, pick the best, describe a prototype, name it, segment the market, write slogans, a 500-word memo, a press release, an inspirational memo, and an HBR-style article outline (Appendix A, PDF pp. 45-46). Baseline task: the same structure for a new drink, without AI.
task.duration: Baseline task 30 minutes; experimental task 90 minutes, with subjects required to stay for the full time (PDF p. 11)

outcomes.name: Creativity rating of each subject's idea list (question 1, shoe ideas)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Appendix D: 'We obtained evaluations of each subject's idea list along the dimension of creativity, ranging from 1 to 10'. Who rated is not stated in Appendix D; the main grading used two human graders from BCG or MBA students (PDF p. 13, fn 6). The 'Table 1' that Appendix D cites for these results is not in the PDF. Measure coded human_raters on the assumption that these are the human grades; the appendix does not say so.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Access to ChatGPT (GPT Only and GPT + Overview, not separated in the text)
contrasts.reported: No numbers printed. Text: 'The idea lists provided by subjects with access to ChatGPT are evaluated as having significantly higher quality than those subjects without ChatGPT.' The cited Table 1 is missing from the PDF.

outcomes.name: Between-subject semantic similarity of shoe ideas (question 1)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each of a subject's roughly 10 ideas is encoded with Google's Universal Sentence Encoder (512 dimensions). For each idea, the average inner product with all ideas of other subjects in the same condition is computed, then averaged over the subject's ideas to give a subject-level 'between semantic similarity'. Higher similarity means less variation. Figure 6 caption calls the measure 'Average Within-Subject Semantic Similarity', but Appendix D defines it as between-subject.

contrasts.reported: Density plot by condition with a dashed vertical line at each condition's mean; no numbers, SEs, or tests printed. Similarity is higher (diversity lower, sign reversed) in GPT Only than in Control. Text: 'there is a marked reduction in the variability of these ideas compared to those not using AI.'
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 36, Figure 6 (printed p. 32); PDF p. 16 (printed p. 12), Section 3.1; PDF pp. 52-53, Appendix D and its Figure 1

contrasts.reported: Same figure. Mean similarity line for GPT + Overview lies to the right of (above) Control, so diversity is lower (sign reversed). No numbers printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 36, Figure 6; PDF p. 53, Appendix D Figure 1

contrasts.treatment_arm: GPT No Humans (100 independent simulated ChatGPT sessions answering the question-1 prompt)
contrasts.control_arm: Human conditions (Control, GPT Only, GPT + Overview)
contrasts.reported: The simulated AI-only condition has the highest similarity of all four conditions in the figure; no numbers printed. Appendix D text calls this simulated condition 'GPT Only', a label also used for a human arm.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 36, Figure 6 notes; PDF pp. 52-53, Appendix D Results

diversity_detail.metric: Subject-level mean inner product (semantic similarity) between each of the subject's ideas and all ideas of other subjects in the same condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against all ideas of other subjects within the same experimental condition, averaged over the subject's ideas
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported: only density plots with condition means as dashed lines; no SE, interval, or test
diversity_detail.notes: Only question 1 (at least 10 shoe ideas) is analyzed. Appendix D text contains a typo ('subjects without access to ChatGPT tend to produce ideas with less semantic similarity ... than those without access'). Ordering in the figure, lowest to highest mean similarity: Control, GPT + Overview, GPT Only, GPT No Humans.

outcomes.name: Quality: composite human-graded score across the 18 questions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each answered question graded by two human graders (BCG staff or MBA students at a top program, PDF p. 13 fn 6); question score = mean of the two grades; composite = mean over questions. Scale 1-10 (Figure 5 notes). The 18 questions cover creativity, analytical thinking, writing, and persuasiveness, so the composite is overall quality, not creativity alone. Robustness: Table 1 columns 2-3 add baseline score and controls; 54 per-question regressions with human grades (pooled AI arms) all significant, mean effect 1.69 (46.6 percent over control mean), Figure 3, PDF p. 33 and PDF p. 14.

contrasts.reported: Table 1 col (1): GPT Only 1.556*** (0.080); control mean 4.099; N = 385; robust SEs. Col (2) 1.585 (0.077); col (3) 1.592 (0.078). Text: 'GPT Only led to a 1.56, or 38% increase.'
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 38, Table 1 (printed p. 34); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 10)

contrasts.reported: Table 1 col (1): GPT + Overview 1.746*** (0.074); control mean 4.099; N = 385; R2 0.598. Col (2) 1.752 (0.070); col (3) 1.769 (0.075). Text: '1.75 increase in scores over the control mean of 4.1, which is a 42.5% increase'.

outcomes.name: Quality (GPT): composite GPT-4-graded score across the 18 questions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4 scored each question; composite = mean over questions. Table 1 col (4) includes Assessment (GPT) and controls. Robustness: 54 per-question regressions with GPT grades, mean effect 1.36 (20.2 percent), Figure 4, PDF p. 34 and PDF p. 14.

contrasts.reported: Table 1 col (4): GPT Only 1.216*** (0.059); control mean 7.207; N = 385; robust SEs. Text: 16.8% increase.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 38, Table 1 col (4); PDF p. 14

contrasts.reported: Table 1 col (4): GPT + Overview 1.349*** (0.058); control mean 7.207; N = 385; F-test GPT = GPT + Overview p = 0.049. Text: 18.6% increase.

participants.quote: The other half (373 consultants) engaged in business problem-solving tasks using quantitative data, customer and company interviews, and including a persuasive writing component.
participants.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 6); Table 4, PDF p. 41

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 (end of April 2023), default system prompt and temperature

task.description: Analytical business case: pick which of three brands the CEO should invest in, using spreadsheet data and interview notes, and suggest tactical actions, in a 500-750 word note (Appendix A, PDF pp. 44-45). The task has a correct answer that GPT-4 was designed to miss.
task.duration: Baseline and experimental tasks 60 minutes each, could finish early (PDF p. 11)

outcomes.name: Recommendation quality (1-10 rubric)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Scored 1-10 by two sets of human graders (BCG consultants not in the experiment; business-school students with grading experience) with an author rubric on tactical actions (Appendix B, PDF pp. 46-48). Coded question 'none' because the task is analytical problem solving with a correct answer, not a creative or ideation task. Correctness (binary) is the paper's primary outcome for this experiment and is not listed.

Table 6 col (1): GPT + Overview 1.475*** (0.242); control mean 5.856; N = 372; F-test GPT = GPT + Overview p = 0.098.

company_involvement.description: Run with Boston Consulting Group: three authors are BCG staff, BCG collected the data and passed it to the authors, and Lakhani advises BCG on AI strategy. Funding in part from Harvard Business School.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 4), Introduction ('the author team received the data that the company collected'); PDF p. 3, title-page footnote; PDF p. 2

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned 385 analyzed consultants to GPT-4 access (two arms) or no AI on a product-ideation task. Outcomes are scored on their output: human-graded quality across 18 questions (Table 1), a 1-10 creativity rating of the idea list (Appendix D, no numbers printed), and USE-based similarity across subjects' ideas (Figure 6, figure only). Per-arm counts are not reported, and the creativity-specific results lack printed statistics in this working-paper version.

one_line_finding: Among 385 BCG consultants developing a new shoe product, GPT-4 access raised the human-graded quality score by 1.556 (SE 0.080, GPT Only) and 1.746 (SE 0.074, GPT + Overview) over a control mean of 4.099 (PDF p. 38, Table 1), while the semantic similarity of their shoe ideas across subjects rose in both AI arms (PDF p. 36, Figure 6, no statistics printed).
open_questions: The file is the September 2023 working paper; the Organization Science (2026) version may add statistics for the similarity and creativity-rating results or drop them. Extraction should check the version of record.
Appendix D cites a 'Table 1' with creativity ratings of idea lists that is not in this PDF; who rated creativity and the numbers are unknown.
Per-arm sample sizes are not reported anywhere; the 94 consultants who answered the enrollment survey but did not complete may or may not have been randomized.

Design class: the paper calls it a field experiment (company-run, realistic tasks, bonus-related recognition), but the tasks used a fictional company in a separate 5-hour session; field_rct versus lab_rct may need a decision.
Construct for the composite Quality score: it mixes creativity, analytical, writing, and persuasion questions; coded usefulness (quality) rather than overall_creativity.
notes: PDF page numbers are the file's page numbers; main-text printed page numbers are 4 lower (e.g., Table 1 is printed p. 34, PDF p. 38). The markdown conversion stops partway through Table 1 (PDF p. 38), so Tables 2-6 and Appendices A-E were read from the PDF. Outcomes not listed because they bear on none of the three questions: S1 percent of tasks completed (Table 2) and time to reach the last question (Table 3); S2 correctness (Table 4: GPT + Overview -0.245, SE 0.054; GPT Only -0.139, SE 0.053; control mean 0.844; N = 373) and timing (Table 5). Appendix C (retainment of GPT text) is descriptive among AI users only. Appendix E (Centaur and Cyborg practices) is qualitative, describing '244 professional consultants as they used AI to complete a real-world, analytic task' (PDF p. 55).
